tweets.body:
An agent saves a successful procedure, then reuses it after the environment changes. I think lifelong learning needs a maintenance loop around skills: test whether they transfer, preserve the evidence, and retire them when they stop working. 

This is a question we are exploring at MidBrain: how experience becomes a reusable procedure, and how that procedure stays valid across sessions and tools. I would like to compare notes with builders whose agents keep applying yesterday’s fix to today’s task

tweets.body:
This one is personal for me too.

@Thom_Wolf , thank you for backing @MidbrainAI  and our vision early. thank you for meeting me at @SlushHQ. And especially for taking the time to talk with me on WhatsApp when we were at a real crossroads with the company.

Those conversations matter more than people realize. Especially when you’re building something that still sounds a little crazy and the path isn’t obvious yet.

And @davidhelgason , thank you for facilitating that first encounter. A single introduction can sometimes alter the trajectory of a company.

This is a huge moment for European founders.

What @Thom_Wolf, @ClementDelangue , @julien_c  and the @huggingface team built started in Europe and became part of the basic infrastructure of modern AI.

And now, together with @nvidia, I think they have a shot at building the strongest open source AI platform in the world.

@nvidia brings compute and massive resources. @huggingface brings the models, datasets, tooling, research culture and, maybe most importantly, the community of people actually building with this technology.

Put those together and you get something I find genuinely exciting: more of the raw materials of AI becoming accessible to builders.more models. More tools. More compute. More experimentation.

Less of AI being something only a handful of giant labs can build with.

There’s also something important here for Europe.

We talk a lot about Europe being great at research but bad at turning research into global technology companies. About talent leaving. About capital. About regulation. About whether the next generation of foundational companies can really be built from here.

@huggingface is a pretty strong answer.

You can start here. You can think globally from day one. You can build around openness and community rather than keeping everything behind closed doors. And you can end up defining how an entire generation of developers works with AI.

Very happy for Thomas, Clem, Julien and everyone at Hugging Face.

And excited by the larger idea behind this.

Give people the models, tools, compute and knowledge to build.

Then see what millions of people create.

tweets.title: If I correct an agent today, I do not just want that correction stored somewhere. I want it to affect how the agent behaves tomorrow, next week, and ideally mon
tweets.body:
If I correct an agent today, I do not just want that correction stored somewhere. I want it to affect how the agent behaves tomorrow, next week, and ideally months later, even as the task, the project, and the surrounding context keep changing.

The same should be true for successful procedures, failed attempts, changing preferences, new evidence, and instructions that are no longer valid. Some experiences should become more important over time, some should be revised, and some should gradually lose authority.

Can an AI accumulate experience over time, understand which parts of that experience still matter, and actually become better because of it?

tweets.body:
16 years ago today, on 26 August 2010, I left Romania.

I had a guitar, a few bags, and a pretty clear plan: I was going to become a rockstar.

Reality had other plans.

For a while I was basically homeless in Copenhagen, sleeping in the airport, hiding from security guards and playing guitar to get by.

Snap back to reality, here comes gravity.

I eventually landed at Aalborg University Copenhagen.

Music became engineering, then interaction design, cognitive science, gaming and UX.

I met the founders of @unity and started experimenting with real-time 3D. I worked around The Eye Tribe - later acquired by Oculus/Meta - obsessed with eye tracking, attention and emotion.

Then came VR.

That obsession took me to @volvocars, where a few experiments became a decade of pioneering XR and leading innovation inside one of the world's most traditional industries.

Together with @varjodotcom and incredible teams, we put mixed reality into moving cars, built digital twins, and simulated situations too dangerous, expensive or rare to test in reality.

Somewhere along the way I realised I was never really obsessed with VR.

I was obsessed with reducing the friction between humans and technology.

That question kept expanding:

from interfaces to experiences,
from experiences to systems,
from “how should this product work?”
to “what world are we actually trying to create?”
That pulled me into systems thinking and foresight.

I worked with Alex McDowell and learned to use worldbuilding to turn dreams into possible futures, futures into scenarios, scenarios into decisions - and eventually decisions into things we could build.

Through @Festival_Cannes, @sxsw, @EU_Commission and many other collaborations, I started bringing artists, engineers, scientists, designers, philosophers and executives into the same room.

I taught at universities, worked with startups, advised founders, invested in some, and found myself on stages around the world talking about this strange journey and what I was learning along the way.

For years these looked like different careers:

musician, coder, researcher, UX designer, XR nerd, corporate innovator, futurist, teacher, investor, founder.

Now they look like the same thread.

Turning data into insight.

Dreams into foresight.

Technology into experiences.

Complexity into something humans can understand and use.

Today that thread has brought me to @MidBrainAI.

Another version of the same problem: building machines that don't just respond, but remember, learn from experience and build continuity with the humans around them.

Looking at that first photo from 2010 is surreal.

I had absolutely no idea where I was going.

Maybe that was the useful part.

Most of the important things didn't come from a career plan.

They came from curiosity, collisions between disciplines, people who opened doors, doors I pushed open myself, and being willing to become a beginner again.

16 years.

Romania → Copenhagen → music → engineering → games → eye tracking → XR → automotive → foresight → art → startups → investing → AI

Quite a journey.

And somehow, it still feels like the beginning.

tweets.title: A company brain contains more than documents. It contains decisions, rejected approaches, customer context, operational procedures, and corrections made by name
tweets.body:
A company brain contains more than documents. It contains decisions, rejected approaches, customer context, operational procedures, and corrections made by named people.

Sending that history to a hosted memory service creates a second question after retrieval quality: who can inspect the memory, who can alter it, and who can reconstruct a customer’s history from the index?

End-to-end encryption changes the architecture. The service can store and search within an access-controlled system, while the organization retains control of the keys and the boundaries between projects, users, and customers.

The unresolved engineering work: encrypted search, key rotation, revocation, provenance, update validation, and useful retrieval without turning the server into a plaintext observer.

tweets.title:
A group of researchers from @UIUC, @Stanford, @Google , @Meta  and around twenty other labs just published a survey covering 218 papers on agent memory.
I spent
tweets.body:
A group of researchers from @UIUC, @Stanford, @Google , @Meta  and around twenty other labs just published a survey covering 218 papers on agent memory.
I spent some time reading it because a surprising amount of the framing overlaps with how we have been thinking about @MidbrainAI  internally.

The survey separates agent memory into episodic memory for what happened, semantic memory for what is known, and procedural memory for how to act. It also describes agents as a foundation model combined with the surrounding agent system and a memory layer that carries information across sessions. We have been using a very similar decomposition in our own work for some time.
A few parts were especially close to problems we have been working on.

The comparison of external-memory systems points to retrieval precision as a weakness of systems such as Mem0 and Zep, particularly because results depend heavily on embeddings and ranking. This is also where our SmartSearch work started. In long conversational memory, retrieving a reasonable set of candidates is often manageable. Deciding which of those memories is actually relevant enough to bring back into context is harder.

The later sections of the survey get closer to the part I find quite interesting: memory management as something the agent itself can learn.

An agent has to decide whether a new experience should be stored, whether an existing memory should be updated, whether two experiences should be consolidated, whether something has become irrelevant, and sometimes whether nothing should happen at all. The survey discusses reinforcement learning and trainable controllers for these decisions. This is very close to the direction of our own online-learning work, where the value comes from improving how experience changes future behaviour over time.

The paper is also fairly open about what is still unresolved. Continual learning without catastrophic forgetting remains difficult. Privacy and trust become much harder once memory persists across long periods. Benchmarking is also still weak when the question is whether an agent actually accumulates useful experience and reuses it safely across many interactions, rather than performing well on a fixed retrieval benchmark.

Those are problems we spend a lot of time on as well, including encrypted memory for environments where the underlying data cannot simply be sent somewhere else.

For anyone working on long-running agents, the survey is useful because it puts a large part of the current memory literature in one place and shows how much of the work is starting to move from storing and retrieving information toward managing experience over time.

There is still a lot that is unresolved, which is probably the most useful part of the paper.

tweets.title:
An agent got 15.3x slower when someone deleted one text file.

Same model. Same weights. Same world. The Voyager ablation removed the skill library and the agen
tweets.body:
An agent got 15.3x slower when someone deleted one text file.

Same model. Same weights. Same world. The Voyager ablation removed the skill library and the agent needed over fifteen times as long to hit the same Minecraft milestones. The learning was never in the model. It lived in an artifact the model reads.

Micheal Lanham wrote a sharp piece on this yesterday, and it hit close to home. We ran into the same wall in @Minecraft  two years ago.

We built a composite architecture for long-horizon agents. A fast policy that proposed actions cheaply. A slow controller that planned, verified, and replanned when things broke. Multiple processes running in parallel on different clocks, the way a brain does. System 1 and System 2, wired together.

It worked. For exactly one session.

The next day the agent repeated every mistake it had already solved. The deliberation never compounded. Reflections were generated, used once, discarded. We had built a System 2 agent with the memory of a goldfish.

The missing piece was never a smarter model. It was consolidation. A loop that takes today's deliberation and turns it into tomorrow's reflex. Biology runs it during sleep: replay the high-salience episodes, compress them into procedure, let the noise decay. When we added it, our agents stopped relearning and started improving. Fear memories even generalized to entirely new world seeds.

The field is now converging on the same architecture from the infrastructure side. Skills as procedural memory. Reflection moved off the request path into offline consolidation passes. Small diffs instead of full rewrites, because a memory store the model keeps regenerating degrades like a photocopy of a photocopy.

And ablation as a discipline: turn the memory layer off for a slice of traffic and measure what breaks. On interdependent multi-session benchmarks, removing active memory roughly halves task completion.

We carried that loop from Minecraft into embodied agents, and it is now the core of our continual learning research at MidBrain. Episodic traces. Semantic abstractions. Procedural consolidation. Salience decides what moves up and what decays.

Storing isn't learning. Learning is what survives the night.

One question, and I want a number, not a vibe: have you ever run your agent with memory switched off, and what did it cost you?

Links in comments.

tweets.body:
I used @unity  for everything from games and art experiments to eye-tracking research, industrial simulations and digital twins.

when I started at  @volvocars , that eventually meant combining @unity  with @varjodotcom  to build mixed-reality driving experiences, placing real cars, people and physical controls inside virtual test environments.

You could sit in an actual vehicle, drive on a physical track, and see an entirely different world through the headset. New roads, traffic scenarios, interfaces and behaviours could be tested before they existed anywhere else.

That moment never really got old: taking something that only existed on a screen, putting on the headset, and suddenly standing inside it.

These days, I spend more time thinking about how machines remember and learn from experience.

But a lot of that curiosity started here-building worlds, entering them, and seeing how people and technology behaved once they shared the same reality.

tweets.body:
Strongly agree. I think the framing of “text optimization” is actually exposing a deeper distinction between slow learning and fast learning.

Weights are crystallized experience. Text, memory, procedures, and external artifacts are active experience.

Human intelligence has always relied on both. Civilization itself is arguably a giant external memory system built from books, maps, laws, scientific papers, and code.
